text: My inbox shows 212 unread messages and two calendar alerts are blinking in the corner of the monitor. I open the first email, then a chat window pops up asking for a file I haven't finished, so I switch tabs. The printer in the hall jams again, and I walk over to pull out a crumpled page I never asked for.

Three people stand at my desk with questions, and the phone on my left keeps lighting up with a number I don't recognize. I type half a reply to the client, delete it, and start again. The slide deck I promised by noon still has blank pages where the charts should be, and the clock above the door says 11:40.

Every time I finish a line of the spreadsheet, another request lands in my messages. I copy numbers from one window into another, check the totals, and find an error from the morning that I have to trace back row by row. My coffee has gone cold beside the keyboard.

The meeting ran long, so I sit down with the stack of forms that were due yesterday. I sign the first page, then notice the date field is wrong on the next four. My pen keeps skipping across the paper, and the reception phone rings again from the desk outside.

Dinner for six starts at seven and I have three pans going with nothing finished. The rice is boiling over the side of the pot, the chicken needs flipping, and I can't find the lid to the beans. I move from burner to burner, turning every knob to a different number.

Lunch was supposed to take twenty minutes, but the bread is stale and the tomatoes are still in the bag. I cut one slice, drop it, and cut another while the cheese slides off the counter. I eat standing up, one hand on the fridge door, and my plate is still half full when the bell rings.

The grocery order arrived with the wrong milk and no eggs, and the recipe calls for both in the first step. I open the cupboard, count what is left, and then open it again. The bowl on the counter fills with flour I measured twice, and the oven beeps to say it reached temperature before I've even started.

Breakfast is a row of plates on the counter: toast for the kids, eggs for my partner, oats for me, none of them started. The kettle hisses, a lunch box needs a name label, and the dog is sitting by the back door. I put bread in the toaster, forget it, and smell it turning black.

The bus is late, so I'm standing in the rain with my bag, a phone at six percent, and a message from my manager asking where I am. Two buses come in the wrong direction. I check the route map three times, the screen fogs, and my shoes soak through at the curb.

I'm merging onto the motorway with a lorry close behind and a sat nav voice telling me to turn left at the next junction. The lane splits, I miss the exit, and the car behind honks. I glance at the child's school bag sliding across the back seat and the petrol light flashing on the dashboard.

Traffic on the ring road has stopped completely, and my phone buzzes on the passenger seat with three reminders I haven't read. I have a parking ticket to pay, a rental to return, and groceries that will spoil in the boot. I edge forward a car length, then stop again, and the engine ticks as it idles.

The train doors close on my coat sleeve, so I pull free and step onto the platform with a folder slipping from my arms. Papers scatter across the wet tiles. I gather them while commuters push past, then realise my pass is missing from my pocket.

The tent poles won't click into place, and the wind keeps pulling the nylon out of my hands. I've got a map, a headtorch, and a cup of cold tea balanced on a stone. Clouds are building over the ridge, and I've forgotten the stakes for the back corner.

The garden is overgrown after a month away, with bindweed wrapped around the beans and slugs in every bed. I pull at roots, drop the trowel, and find another patch of nettles under the hedge. The hose only reaches half the rows, and the water runs off the hard clay.

The path up the hill is slick with mud, and the dog keeps circling back to chase a stick I can't reach. I check my watch, count the miles on my phone, and realise the sun drops behind the trees earlier than I planned. My boots fill with water at every step.

Rain comes sideways through the allotment gate while I try to cover the seedlings with fleece. The pegs slip, the plastic sheet tears, and the wheelbarrow tips over in the mud. I kneel by the first row, press the corners down, and watch the next gust lift the corner again.

The laundry basket has spilled onto the hall floor, and half of it is still in the washer, sour from yesterday. I load a second machine, pull out a shirt that's already damp, and hang it on the radiator beside a wet towel. Dust drifts from the skirting boards every time I walk past.

I start the vacuum in the living room, but the cord is caught under the sofa, so I unplug it and pull it free. Crumbs cover the rug, a glass sits by the window, and the bin is overflowing with yesterday's post. I empty one drawer, then the next, and stack everything on the stairs.

The bathroom sink is blocked, the drain is gurgling, and the mop bucket still has dirty water from the hallway. I scrub the tiles, rinse the cloth, and find the cupboard door hanging off its hinge. Each job I finish makes room for two more on the list stuck to the fridge.

Three loads of dishes sit on the counter, and the sink has gone grey from the pan I soaked overnight. I stack plates on the rack, but the bottom ones are still wet, so I shift them again. The bin needs taking out, the mat needs shaking, and the window cleaner is empty.

The waiting room is full, and the receptionist asks for my insurance card while I'm still juggling my coat and a folder of test results. I fill out the form on a clipboard, but the pen has run dry, so I borrow one from the man beside me. My name is called twice before I notice.

The pharmacist asks me to repeat my date of birth, and the queue behind me is growing. My prescription is out of stock, the bottle label is in the wrong name, and the bag of pills I already paid for has vanished. I stand at the counter reading the same sheet three times.

The appointment letter says ten, but the clinic moved rooms and nobody updated the board. I climb two flights of stairs with a folder of scans, then realise the lift is out. A nurse asks which arm the last blood test used, and I can't remember the date on the form.

The blood pressure cuff tightens, and the number on the screen climbs before the nurse writes it down. She asks about my sleep, my medication, and whether I've eaten today, and I answer while flipping through a pile of printed forms. My phone rings in my pocket, and I can't reach it.

My sister's birthday party is at my place in an hour, and the cake is still in the box on the hall table. The kids are pulling streamers off the wall, the oven timer goes off, and my brother has just asked where the corkscrew is. I hand him the bottle opener and go back for the candles.

My mother calls while I'm on the bus home, asking why I didn't reply to her message from last week. I try to explain the rota at work, the school form that's overdue, and the bill that arrived twice. She keeps talking over me, and my phone is at ten percent.

The group chat has forty unread messages about Saturday's plans, and nobody agrees on the venue. Someone wants to split the bill, someone else wants a different date, and my friend keeps sending photos of the restaurant menu. I type a reply, delete it, type another, and watch the three dots appear again.

We're packing up after my nephew's sleepover, and there are sleeping bags on every chair. One child is crying about a missing sock, another has spilled juice on the rug, and the car keys have disappeared into the coat pile. I carry three bags to the door and forget which one holds the lunchboxes.

The exam paper is face down on the desk, and the clock on the wall shows twenty minutes left. I've read question four three times, but the numbers won't line up with the formula in my notes. My pencil snaps, I pick up a second one, and the girl beside me coughs.

My essay is due at midnight, and the library printer prints only half of each page. I scroll through twelve browser tabs, copy a quote into the wrong paragraph, and find my reference list has lost its formatting. The vending machine eats my coins, and the battery light on my laptop starts blinking.

The seminar leader asks us to present, and my slides are still in a file I can't open on the classroom computer. I hand round the printed handout, which has the wrong page numbers, and the projector flickers on and off. Someone asks a question about the reading I haven't finished.

Homework for three subjects is spread across the kitchen table, next to a school bag that won't close. My son needs help with fractions, my daughter's project glue has dried in the tube, and the permission slip is still unsigned. I write the date on the first page, cross it out, and write it again.

The running club starts at six, but my trainers are in the car and the rain is coming down in sheets. I jog to the park, my watch buzzes with a missed message, and my legs feel heavy after the first hill. I stop beside the bench, lean on my knees, and check the time again.

The gym's treadmill beside me keeps speeding up, and the screen says I've burned fifty calories when I've only walked a block. I reset the timer, grab a towel, and drop my water bottle on the mat. Music thumps from the speakers while the queue for the weights grows behind me.

The swimming lesson is over, but I still can't find the locker key, and the changing room is filling with wet kids. My goggles snapped at the strap, my swim cap is inside out, and the attendant wants me to move my bag from the bench. I pull the wrong towel from the pile.

My football boots are missing, the match is starting in ten minutes, and the coach is waving me to the touchline. I pull on the spare pair, which are two sizes too big, and tie the laces twice. The ball rolls past my feet while I fumble with the shin pads.

The bike chain slipped off the rear cog, and the wrench keeps slipping off the bolt. I wipe grease onto my jeans, dig for the spare links in a jar of screws, and realise the back wheel is wobbling. Every fix reveals another loose part, so I lay them out in a row on the workbench.

Water drips steadily from the tap into the sink, and the washer I bought doesn't fit the thread. I turn off the water, unscrew the handle, and a spring shoots across the tiles. I crawl under the basin with a torch in my teeth, and the old pipe joint starts weeping again.

The wooden shelf I'm building has three brackets in the wrong place, and the drill battery is nearly flat. Glue has squeezed out of every joint, and the clamps won't hold the side panel square. I measure again, pencil a new mark, then find the saw cut sits a finger's width off.

My knitting has a dropped stitch three rows down, and the yarn is splitting every time I pull it through. I unravel the last section, count the loops again, and lose my place on the chart. The cat keeps batting at the ball of wool on my lap, and the pattern sheet curls up on the arm of the chair.

The post office queue reaches the door, and the clerk says my parcel needs a signature I didn't give. I have a bank form to hand in, a library book overdue, and a prescription I still need to collect by five. My bag is heavy on one shoulder, and the card reader keeps timing out.

The supermarket trolley wheel jams at the entrance, and my list has been rewritten on the back of an envelope. I push past the tinned goods, double back for the oat milk, and find the aisle for bin bags is blocked by a pallet. The receipt printer behind the till runs out of paper while I'm still unpacking.

My phone shows the parcel tracking has changed twice, and the pick-up shop closes in twenty minutes. I drive across town with the petrol light on, park in the wrong bay, and hurry in with a torn envelope. The shop assistant points to the back wall, where a long line already waits.

The hardware shop has no screws in the size on my list, and the man at the counter is answering a call. I search three aisles, check the plastic tubs for the right thread, and pick up a bag of hinges I didn't need. My receipt is still in the car, and the dog I left outside is barking.

The airport gate has changed twice in ten minutes, and my boarding pass says I'm in group six. My passport is in the outer pocket of the bag I already checked, and the queue for security wraps around the pillars. I walk fast with my coat over my arm and the charger cable dangling from my hand.

The hotel receptionist says my reservation is for next week, and the room I booked has been given to someone else. My suitcase wheel has come off in the lobby, the taxi is idling outside, and my phone shows a dead map. I drag the case across the marble with one hand and hold the printed confirmation with the other.

The bus to the coast was cancelled, so I'm waiting at a station where the timetable board is blank. My ticket won't scan at the barrier, and the next train is full of people carrying bikes and prams. I count the coins in my pocket, then the stops left on the route, and the light is fading.

I've been on the ferry for three hours and the crossing keeps getting longer, while the cafe has sold out of sandwiches. My phone signal drops, the hotel email I need is stuck in the outbox, and the luggage hold door is locked. I stand on the deck with my backpack, watching the grey harbour get no closer.

The piano lid is open, and the sheet music for the recital piece is in three different folders. My left hand misses the chord on the third line, the metronome keeps ticking faster, and my fingers slip on the same bar every time. I flip back to the start, lose the page, and try again from the top.

The canvas is propped on the easel, and the paint on my palette has dried into a crust. I mix a new blue, smear it across the sky, and the wrong green creeps into the hills. Brushes lie across the windowsill, and the light is shifting while I stand in front of the same corner.

The choir rehearsal starts in ten minutes, and I still can't find the second page of my part. The conductor counts us in, the altos are flat, and the pianist keeps stopping to correct a bar. My music stand wobbles as I turn the sheet, and the score slides onto the floor.

My pottery wheel is spinning too fast, and the clay keeps sliding off-centre under my palms. I add water, press harder, and the wall of the bowl caves in. I scrape the mess into a bucket, wipe the splashes from the wall, and set the next lump on the wheel.

My laptop freezes on the video call, the screen stuck on a frame of my boss's face. The slide file won't open, my password is rejected for the third time, and a pop-up asks me to update the software. I restart the machine, and the cursor spins while the call keeps going without me.

Storage on the phone is full, so the camera refuses to take the photo I need for the form. I delete old messages, clear the cache, and watch the progress bar crawl across the screen. Three apps crash on restart, and the charger cable keeps slipping out of the socket by the bed.

The email server has bounced my message back to me twice, and the attachment is too big to send. I compress the file, upload it to the wrong folder, and find the link I sent has expired. My notifications keep stacking up along the top of the screen, one above another.

The printer driver won't install, and the spreadsheet I need for the meeting has crashed twice. I reboot the router, reconnect the wifi, and get a message saying the network password has changed. Every time I try a new fix, the old error flashes back up on the screen.
